tldr: On a budget $300 quadruped with a severe 76 ms transport latency, reinforcement learning with an LSTM naturally discovered a central pattern generator (CPG) akin to a biological spinal cord, enabling stable real-world locomotion without complex state observers.
hero_caption: A comparison between low-cost toy-grade servo motors and expensive research-grade actuators. (a) The $300 Mini Pupper 2 used in this work uses $8 brushed DC servos. Serial communication via an ESP32 introduces a massive 76 ms latency and limits feedback to coarse position only. (b) In contrast, research robots costing thousands to tens of thousands of dollars provide instantaneous torque and velocity with less than 5 ms of latency. How to bridge this hardware gap through software is the core problem addressed in this paper.
overview:
In recent years, reinforcement learning (RL) for quadrupedal locomotion has made remarkable strides. However, most of these dazzling successes have relied on expensive, high-end machines equipped with high-performance actuators like quasi-direct drive motors. These premium robots have almost no latency (<5 ms) and can provide high-precision feedback of joint velocities and torques.

On the other hand, trying to deploy an RL policy onto a budget hobby quadruped costing around $300 (such as the Mini Pupper 2) hits a devastating wall. The actuators are cheap brushed servos, and due to the communication pipeline, there is a massive 76 ms transport delay between sending a command and the actuator reaching it. Moreover, the sensors only return coarse joint positions—neither joint velocity nor torque is available. Because of this, standard RL policies that assume a Markov decision process (MDP) fail to walk on the real hardware entirely.

To overcome this, the authors drew inspiration from neuroscience and biology. Biological nervous systems also face substantial latencies of 100 to 160 ms in signal transmission from the brain to muscles and sensory feedback. Animals can still run because "central pattern generators" (CPGs) in their spinal cords produce autonomous rhythmic gaits, avoiding over-reliance on delayed and noisy sensory signals.

Taking cues from this biological mechanism, the authors built a simulation environment incorporating the 76 ms latency and compared four network architectures: MLP, LSTM, GRU, and Transformer. They found that only the LSTM, with its shift-register-like inductive bias that preserves past hidden states linearly, naturally learned and emerged an autonomous rhythm (CPG) without any explicit periodic reward. Furthermore, by predicting the nonlinear behavior of real servos using small per-joint MLPs and running a largely open-loop pipeline that drops corrupted sensor feedback, they achieved stable walking on budget hardware with virtually no additional parameter tuning.
contributions: Built a complete Sim-to-Real pipeline that achieves physical locomotion on a budget quadruped (Mini Pupper 2) burdened with extreme 76 ms actuator transport delay and missing sensor feedback.

Demonstrated via dynamical systems analysis that training an LSTM with RL in a delayed environment leads to the natural emergence of an autonomous limit cycle (CPG) like a biological spinal cord, without explicit rhythmic rewards or structural priors.

Uncovered a noise crossover phenomenon (threshold $\sigma \approx 0.2$ rad) through per-joint noise ablation experiments, showing that zeroing observation feedback on degraded hardware yields more stable locomotion than using noisy measurements.
Proposed an optimal separation of models across hierarchical timescales, using an LSTM for long-horizon transport delay compensation and stateless MLPs for short-horizon servo dynamics prediction.

sections.heading: Breaking the Luxury Robot Privilege: The 76 ms Chasm Faced by Budget Hardware
sections.summary: RL locomotion successes rely heavily on expensive hardware, while budget robots struggle with massive transport latencies and missing sensor data. This challenge closely mirrors the delay biological nervous systems face, and formalizing it as a POMDP provides the path to a solution.
sections.details:
Quadrupedal RL locomotion demos have captured worldwide attention, but most are performed on research platforms costing $10,000 to $150,000. These platforms feature expensive quasi-direct drive (QDD) motors with sub-5 ms latency, providing high-fidelity torque, velocity, and position feedback. In other words, they buy latency reduction and observation fidelity with money.

In contrast, affordable robots for education and hobbies—such as the $300 Mini Pupper 2—run on $8 brushed DC servo motors. Routing commands through serial communication on a microcontroller (ESP32) introduces a 76 ms transport delay before instructions reach the motor. On top of that, the feedback is restricted to quantized joint positions, with no velocity or torque measurements available.

Frequency response measurements on the real hardware (Fig. F2) revealed a constant 76 ms delay across 1 to 6 Hz, with tracking performance deteriorating sharply above 3 Hz. By the time a command arrives, the joint state has already moved elsewhere, causing naive closed-loop feedback control to oscillate wildly.

### I-A Problem Statement
To tackle this problem, should we handcraft an intricate state observer for a simple network, or should we let a time-aware recurrent network learn the delay dynamics internally?

In a system with a $k$-step delay, Markovian properties only hold if the state includes not only the current state $s_t$ but also the unexecuted action history $[a_{t-k}, \dots, a_{t-1}]$. Because joint velocities and torques are unobserved, the task becomes a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP). Inspired by biological nervous systems, which handle 100 to 160 ms feedback delays, the authors investigated how time-aware neural networks can resolve this partial observability.

captions.F2: Delay and frequency response identification of the physical servo motor. Plotting the commanded sinusoidal trajectory (blue dashed) against the actual position (red solid) reveals a constant transport delay of approximately 76 ms from 1 to 6 Hz, with tracking fidelity degrading severely above 3 Hz.

sections.heading: Simulated Learning and Hardware Deployment: Bridging Disparate Timescales
sections.summary: Training was conducted via PPO in NVIDIA Isaac Lab using an actuator model faithfully reproducing the 76 ms latency. Comparing four network architectures showed that only LSTM converged stably. Hardware deployment used a two-layer architecture decoupling the policy from the servo prediction model.
sections.details:
### II-A Training
Training was conducted in NVIDIA Isaac Lab (IsaacSim) using Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), running 4,096 parallel environments on a single RTX 4090. To replicate the measured 76 ms hardware latency, the authors built `DelayedPDActuatorCfg`, which injects 33 to 43 steps of transport delay into the 500 Hz physics simulation.

The observation space is 60-dimensional, comprising base linear and angular velocities, projected gravity vectors, velocity commands, 12 relative joint positions, joint velocities, joint torques, and previous actions.

### II-B Network Architectures
Four architectures—MLP, LSTM, GRU, and Transformer—were compared under identical environments and reward structures without curricula. Surprisingly, only the LSTM achieved stable walking without a curriculum.

- MLP: Failed to converge without a multi-stage curriculum that gradually introduced delays and penalties.
- GRU: Failed completely to learn locomotion despite being recurrent. The GRU applies nonlinear transformations at every step via update gates, preventing it from maintaining a linear "shift register" (delay buffer) path for delayed actions.
- Transformer: Failed to converge within the training budget. For the task of simply holding fixed-step delays, the cell state of the LSTM provides a vastly superior inductive bias.

### II-C Deployment
Deploying to the real robot posed two major challenges: the servos only report position, and issuing commands too quickly causes motor lag and error accumulation. Therefore, the control frequency was reduced to 25 Hz.

Deploying an MLP required a synthetic PD observer to reconstruct missing velocities and torques, demanding manual tuning of more than six parameters (stiffness, damping, inertia, delay stages, etc.).

In contrast, deploying the LSTM was remarkably simple. Instead of using noisy encoder values, the policy fed back joint positions predicted by a small per-joint MLP servo model directly into the next observation, creating a nearly open-loop pipeline. The policy only uses 6 dimensions of real sensor data from the IMU (gyroscope and gravity vector)—just 10% of the total observation—and requires tuning essentially a single parameter: the action scale (0.75x).

sections.heading: Surprising Findings: Emergence of Biological CPGs and the Noise Inversion Phenomenon
sections.summary: The LSTM learned a spinal-cord-like autonomous central pattern generator (CPG) without any periodic reward incentives. Furthermore, noise ablation experiments revealed a striking truth: zeroing out corrupted feedback signals makes the robot walk far more stably.
sections.details:
### III-A Emergent Central Pattern Generator
Training the LSTM produced a remarkable phenomenon: despite receiving no periodic rewards or explicit oscillator structures, the network self-organized an autonomous periodic gait pattern—a central pattern generator (CPG)—within its hidden states (Fig. F4).

Fitting the hardware joint trajectories to a single-frequency sine wave yielded a high coefficient of determination ($R^2=0.77$). All joints synchronized neatly at ~2.8 Hz to produce a coordinated trot gait. This rhythmic gait persisted autonomously even when sensory feedback was severed, while remaining flexible enough to adapt to slopes and steps via IMU gravity vector signals. This mirrors biological CPGs, which maintain walking rhythms when deafferented (sensory inputs removed) and use vestibular signals from the inner ear for balance.

### III-B Robustness to Observation Delay: LSTM vs. MLP
To evaluate delay robustness, the authors conducted stress tests adding up to +320 ms of extra observation delay on top of the 76 ms baseline (Fig. F5). Attractor analysis using Principal Component Analysis (PCA) showed that the LSTM maintained a clean elliptical limit cycle (periodic attractor) in action space even with +320 ms of added delay. In contrast, the MLP trajectory collapsed into a flat line, reducing gait amplitude from 0.49 to 0.16 and quenching oscillations.

### III-C Sim-to-Real Deployment
To determine whether real sensor feedback should actually be used, the authors ran ablation experiments adding Gaussian noise to joint observations (Fig. F7). They discovered a crossover threshold around a standard deviation of $\sigma \approx 0.2$ rad. When noise exceeds this threshold, walking becomes far more stable if observations are zeroed out rather than fed back.

While hardware position noise sat at $\sigma = 0.101$ rad (barely in the useful zone), joint velocity noise computed via finite differences reached $\sigma = 3.17$ rad/s—vastly exceeding the threshold. This velocity noise is precisely why closing the feedback loop failed on budget hardware.

Moreover, the physical servo response deviated heavily from analytical PD models (errors between 0.1 and 1.8 rad). The authors resolved this by using a small per-joint MLP trained on a tiny dataset of just three back-and-forth sweeps (390 samples) as a servo predictor (Fig. F8), slashing error to 0.003–0.03 rad. Using an LSTM for the servo predictor caused overfitting on limited data and drifting predictions that corrupted policy outputs. Pairing an LSTM policy (long-term delay memory) with a stateless MLP servo model (reset every step) was the decisive factor for real-world success.

(b) Thigh joint angles, stance/swing phase diagrams, and commanded actions across all four legs. Without explicit rhythmic rewards, all joints establish a stable trotting rhythm (CPG) at approximately 2.8 Hz.
captions.F5: Limit cycle attractor analysis under diagnostic latency perturbations. Visualizing action space via PCA projections shows that the LSTM (top) maintains a stable elliptical limit cycle under baseline, +160 ms, and +320 ms added delays. In contrast, the MLP (bottom) collapses into a flat band and loses its oscillatory structure as delay increases.
captions.F7: Ablation of joint observation noise versus physical walking performance. A performance crossover occurs around noise standard deviation $\sigma \approx 0.2$ rad, beyond which zeroing out feedback yields superior stability. Physical velocity noise ($\sigma = 3.17$) far exceeds this threshold, making open-loop operation optimal.
captions.F8: Comparison of four observation sources for LSTM deployment. Analytical PD simulation (blue, RMSE 0.1–1.8 rad) diverges significantly from real hardware behavior (red), whereas the data-driven per-joint MLP servo model (yellow, RMSE 0.003–0.03 rad) reproduces the physical servo response with high accuracy.

sections.heading: Why Converge on Nature's Strategy? Architecture Design for Democratic Robotics
sections.summary: In systems with severe latency and noise, overcoming barriers does not require higher hardware precision, but rather selecting the right inductive bias. Assigning distinct timescales across control layers is the key to real-world adaptation.
sections.details:
Training RL policies in simulation has become straightforward, but transferring them to hardware (Sim-to-Real) without high-end platforms has remained exceptionally difficult. The central insight of this work is that instead of buying physical precision with expensive hardware, choosing the right neural network architecture (inductive bias) allows policies to overcome latency and noise.

Just as biological organisms evolved spinal CPGs to handle significant neural conduction delays, training an LSTM in a delayed POMDP environment led to the self-organization of an autonomous oscillator. Architectures like GRUs, where nonlinear gates strongly intervene in hidden state updates, cannot function as "shift registers" that carry past actions unaltered, leading to failure in delay compensation. Transformers, while powerful in theory, carry massive computational overhead unsuitable for edge deployment on low-cost hardware.

Equally important is the architectural principle of matching time horizons to control layers. An autoregressively stable LSTM policy is well-suited for long-term delay compensation and gait maintenance. However, using a recurrent model (LSTM) for short-term servo dynamics causes small prediction errors to accumulate and drift within the autoregressive loop, destabilizing the policy. Placing a stateless MLP with no memory at the short-term prediction layer cleanly severs error propagation.

sections.heading: Conclusion: Opening the Future of Low-Cost Quadrupeds with CPGs
sections.summary: Combining an LSTM policy with a lightweight MLP servo model enabled robust physical walking on a $300 budget robot with 76 ms transport delay. In extreme latency regimes, time-aware networks that generate autonomous biological rhythms provide the fundamental solution.
sections.details:
This paper demonstrated a complete Sim-to-Real pipeline on the Mini Pupper 2, a $300 quadrupedal robot afflicted with 76 ms transport latency and missing sensor feedback.

While running an MLP policy on hardware required a synthetic PD bridge with more than six manually tuned parameters, the LSTM policy autonomously acquired a central pattern generator (CPG) and transferred to the real robot with essentially one tuning knob: the action scale. Dynamical systems attractor analysis and noise ablation experiments provided theoretical and empirical explanations for why the LSTM preserves robust limit cycles under latency perturbations and why degraded sensor feedback should be discarded.

On cost-constrained platforms dominated by transport delays, adopting recurrent architectures with linear memory pathways liberates engineers from tedious manual deployment tuning. This study suggests that in delayed environments, nature's strategy of generating autonomous rhythms represents a universal solution for embodied control.

takeaways: When actuator transport latency is high, using an LSTM policy in RL leads to the natural emergence of an autonomous walking rhythm (CPG) without explicit periodic rewards.
When feedback noise is extreme (exceeding $\sigma \approx 0.2$ rad, like in cheap servos), running open-loop by zeroing observations is more stable than closing the loop with corrupted sensor data.

In multi-layered deployment architectures, recurrent LSTMs excel at global control like policies, whereas stateless MLPs without memory are best for local servo prediction to prevent error accumulation.
You do not need an expensive robot: combining delay-aware POMDP formulation with the right inductive bias (LSTM) unlocks advanced RL locomotion on $300 budget hardware.
limitations: Hardware-induced biases remain: mechanical asymmetries in legs and hip joints, along with IMU gyro drift, cause the robot to drift slightly in a clockwise arc during forward walking.
Training the MLP servo model requires collecting real hardware sweep data beforehand (open-loop replay), and prolonged collection risks damaging cheap servos.
Evaluations focused primarily on flat ground and gentle simulation terrains, leaving dynamic hops on rough terrain or rapid push-recovery capabilities unverified.
